title: Holy water at the door
hook: touching water at the church door recalls your baptism

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sign of the cross, slowly, and the Trinity inside it. Your line was one God, three persons, one gesture. Did you notice anyone make it? Day ninety-eight.

Walk into almost any Catholic church and watch the people ahead of you at the door. Before they've even looked up at the altar, they stop at a small basin fixed to the wall or standing on a pillar. They dip two fingers in, touch forehead, heart, shoulders, and walk on. Kids stretch on their toes to reach it. Some people flick a drop onto a friend. It takes two seconds, and most visitors never ask what it is. It's water. That's all. And it isn't all. Today: holy water at the door.
screen: `A BASIN BY THE DOOR.` → `TWO FINGERS, TWO SECONDS.` → `WATER, AND NOT ONLY WATER.`

segments.voice: The water in that basin has been blessed by a priest, with a prayer asking God to make it a sign of protection and a reminder of baptism. That second part is the key. Nearly every Catholic entered the Church through water. Most were babies, held over a font while a priest poured water three times and said the words you learned yesterday: in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Jesus says in John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "unless a man be born again of water and the Holy Ghost, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God." Paul goes further. He says baptism is like being buried with Christ and rising with him. So when a Catholic walks into church and touches the water, the body is saying: I came in through water once. I'm coming in again. The door of the church echoes the door of baptism. Catholics call holy water a sacramental. That's a different thing from a sacrament. It isn't magic, and it doesn't work by itself. The Church teaches it's a blessed sign that prepares a person to receive grace, through the Church's prayer and the person's own faith. On some Sundays, especially in the Easter season, the priest walks down the aisle and sprinkles the whole congregation with it. People laugh when they get a good splash. Many families also keep a little holy water at home, by the front door or the bed. And this week's thread: a French girl digging for a spring, and now a basin at a door. Water keeps showing up.
screen: `BLESSED WATER, BY THE DOOR.` · `YOU CAME IN THROUGH WATER.` · `A SACRAMENTAL, NOT MAGIC.` · `SPRINKLED ON THE WHOLE CROWD.` · then, large: `BORN AGAIN OF WATER AND THE HOLY GHOST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the water at your tap. If you can, go to a sink, or picture one. Let the water run over your fingers. It isn't holy water. It's a reminder, the way a photo reminds you of a face. If you're Catholic, or you'd like to, touch your forehead with the wet fingers, or make the sign of the cross. If not, just feel the cold, and remember one beginning in your own life. Then sit. The bell holds the time.
Holy water at the door. Water blessed by a priest, touched on the way in, to remember the water of baptism. Today's word.
screen: `HOLY WATER AT THE DOOR — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: every door a baptism. This week ran from Lourdes through four modern saints to the cloud of witnesses, and into the practices. Today, at one doorway, pause for a second, and walk through it like a new start. Day ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Catholics dip their fingers in holy water and make the sign of the cross on entering and often on leaving a church; many keep holy water at home, and at some Sunday Masses the priest sprinkles the congregation with it.

original.note: Latin: blessed water, the Church's old name for holy water.

trapdoor: what you thought: a basin of water by the door.
what it means: blessed water that Catholics touch on the way in, remembering the water they were baptized in.
what a scholar hears: a sacramental, not a sacrament. it prepares for grace through the Church's prayer, and the sprinkling rite at Mass once opened with a psalm verse.

sources.quoted: unless a man be born again of water and the Holy Ghost, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God.

notes: Douay-Rheims John 3:5 fragment given from memory (Challoner: 'Amen, amen I say to thee, unless a man be born again of water and the Holy Ghost, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God'); confirm.
Sacramentals: CCC 1667–1670; the phrasing 'prepares a person to receive grace, through the Church's prayer and the person's own faith' paraphrases 1670. Confirm.
The rite of blessing and sprinkling holy water may replace the penitential act at Sunday Mass, especially in the Easter season; traditionally the Asperges (Psalm 50/51:9). Confirm.
